notes.meaning: Abraham's servant retells how Rebekah quickly lowered her water jar and offered to draw water for him and all ten of his camels. Her cheerful hard work proved she was kind and ready to serve strangers. This exact action showed the servant that God had answered his prayer at the well.

The servant asked about Rebekah's family and learned she was the granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor. Hearing this confirmed she was from Abraham's own kin, fulfilling the oath he had made. The servant then placed the nose ring and heavy gold bracelets on her as tokens of honor.

The servant describes how he bowed down and praised the Lord right there by the spring. He thanked God for guiding him on the true path to find the right young woman for Isaac. True faith always pauses to give thanks when God opens the way.

The servant asks the family for a plain and honest answer to Abraham's request. He wants to know if they will show true loyalty and let Rebekah go, or refuse so he can look elsewhere. A faithful messenger keeps his focus entirely on his master's business.

Laban and Bethuel admit that God has clearly arranged this whole matter from start to finish. Because the Lord had made His will so plain, they could neither argue against it nor change anything. When God's hand is obvious, the only right response is to agree.

The family willingly places Rebekah into the servant's care to become Isaac's wife. They recognize that God Himself has decreed the marriage through these clear events. They surrender their daughter to follow the plan the Lord set in motion.

The moment the servant hears their consent, he bows his face to the dirt in deep reverence to the Lord. Instead of congratulating himself on a successful deal, he gives all the credit to God. Every fresh mercy calls for fresh thanksgiving.

The servant unpacks rich gifts of silver, gold, and fine robes and gives them to Rebekah. He also gives costly presents to her mother and brother as the customary marriage gift. These valuable items showed Abraham's great wealth and his ability to care generously for the bride.

The men finally eat, drink, and rest for the night once their task is arranged. Early the next morning, the servant asks to depart right away back to his master. A diligent worker does not let comfort slow down the work he was sent to finish.

Rebekah's mother and brother ask for her to stay behind for about ten days. They loved her and felt the natural sorrow of parting with her so suddenly. Worldly joys are often touched with the pain of letting go.

The servant urges them not to hold him back, since the Lord had already made the trip a complete success. He feels a sacred urgency to deliver the bride and report back to Abraham. God's blessings should stir us to move forward, not to linger.

The family decides to call Rebekah in and let her speak for herself. While parents guided marriage choices, they did not force their daughters against their will. Rebekah had a personal say in the direction of her own life.

When asked if she is willing to leave right away with this stranger, Rebekah firmly answers, 'I will go.' She trusted that God was calling her into this new home and family. Her bold faith led her to leave everything familiar without hesitation.

The family sends Rebekah away with their blessings, accompanied by her childhood nurse Deborah. Her nurse was a trusted helper and second mother who provided comfort and support on the long trek. This showed the care and honor her family gave her as she left.

Her family pronounces a loving parting blessing over her. They pray that she will have countless descendants and that her children will conquer their enemies. This blessing matches the great promise of victory and many offspring that God gave to Abraham.

Rebekah and her maidservants climb onto the camels and set out behind Abraham's servant. The presence of these attendants shows that her family had wealth and that she had grown up in an honored home. The caravan began the long, quiet trek south toward Canaan.

Isaac was living in the Negev, the dry southern country of Canaan, and had just visited Beer-lahai-roi. That well was famous as the place where God saw and comforted Hagar in her distress. Living near that place of prayer was fitting for Isaac's quiet and trusting walk with God.

Toward evening, Isaac walked out into the open fields to think quietly and pray. As he looked up across the plains, he caught sight of the camels coming in the distance. Quiet times alone in nature help quiet the heart to hear God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the rare Hebrew word translated as 'meditate' might mean 'to lament' or mourn, pointing to Isaac grieving over his mother's death.

notes.meaning: Rebekah looked up and saw Isaac walking toward the caravan. She quickly stepped down from her camel to greet him on foot. In the ancient world, dismounting was a sign of deep respect and courtesy when meeting someone of high standing.

When the servant told her that the walking man was Isaac, Rebekah covered herself with a veil. This veil marked her as a bride presenting herself with modesty and honor to her future husband. It was a sign of her reverence and pure devotion to him.

The servant gave Isaac a complete report of everything that had taken place on his long journey. He explained how God answered his prayer at the well and led him straight to Rebekah. Hearing the story assured Isaac that the Lord had personally chosen his bride.

Isaac brought Rebekah into Sarah's tent, took her as his wife, and loved her deeply. Bringing her into his late mother's tent established her as the new leading woman of the covenant family. In this loving marriage, Isaac finally found comfort after the deep sorrow of his mother's death.
